title: Karma Yoga
hook: a chapter title that sounds backwards: we help ourselves, not the world
carry: the giver is the one who says thank you

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vivekananda in Chicago: the frog in the well, and the monk who said he was sitting in his own well, too: nothing can be bigger than my well. Did you ask one more question? Day nine hundred forty-two.

Saturday morning, a folding table outside a shelter, and a volunteer handing out sandwiches. She's tired, a little proud of herself, and every so often she waits for a thank-you that doesn't come. Vivekananda, back from Chicago and lecturing in America, gave a whole talk about it. Its title sounds backwards: we help ourselves, not the world. Today, Karma Yoga, his book on the yoga of work, and the gratitude that runs the other way.
screen: `A VOLUNTEER WAITS FOR THANKS.` → `A TITLE THAT SOUNDS BACKWARDS.` → `WE HELP OURSELVES, NOT THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Karma Yoga is a set of Vivekananda's talks on work, gathered as a book. In the chapter called We Help Ourselves, Not the World, he starts by taking some air out of the helper. The world isn't waiting for any one of us to rescue it, he says. It will go on, with or without our help. That sounds harsh until you hear where he's going. If the world doesn't need us, then helping is not a favor we do it. It's a chance we're given. He calls the world a great moral gymnasium, where we all exercise so that we grow stronger. The person you help, in that picture, is the one who lets you into the gym. So he turns the usual thank-you around. Don't stand over someone and say, here, poor fellow, take this. Stand thankful that they let you give. The blessing, he says, is to the giver. Then he goes one step further, and this step comes straight from his Vedanta. Serve the person in front of you as you would worship God, because, in the Vedanta he teaches, the divine is present in them. Not pity from above. Worship, from slightly below. Notice what this does to the volunteer at the table. The wait for thanks has nothing to hang on. She isn't owed anything. She's the one who got the workout. And the person taking the sandwich isn't a project. In his picture, they're the one doing her a kindness.
screen: `THE WORLD DOESN'T NEED RESCUING.` · `A GREAT MORAL GYMNASIUM.` · `THE GIVER SAYS THANK YOU.` · `SERVE AS WORSHIP.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath slow. Bring to mind someone you've helped lately: a coworker, a parent, a stranger, a child. Notice if any part of you is still waiting for their thanks, or keeping a small score. No need to scold that part. Then try turning it around, the way the chapter does. Silently thank them for letting you help. See their face as you do. If you pray, you can hold them in a prayer you already know. The bell holds the time.
Karma Yoga. The yoga of work, and Vivekananda's book of talks on it, where the giver is the one who says thank you.
Your line: the giver is the one who says thank you. Today, after you help someone, be the first one to say thank you. Day nine hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Hindu service groups, including those of the Ramakrishna order, describe their work as seva, service offered as worship, and Vivekananda's Karma Yoga is read in Vedanta study circles alongside the Bhagavad Gita.

original.note: Sanskrit: the yoga of action, the path Vivekananda's book describes.

trapdoor: what you thought: karma yoga means doing good deeds.
what it means: doing good so that you are changed, and thanking the one who let you.
what a scholar hears: in the chapter 'we help ourselves, not the world', Vivekananda calls the world a moral gymnasium and service a form of worship.

notes: All paraphrase of Vivekananda's English. Confirm in Karma-Yoga ch. 5: the world goes on without our help; 'a great moral gymnasium'; not giving with 'here, poor man'; the giver being thankful; worshipping the one served as God.
